# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXX. THE GHOST ON THE DYKE

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

In some way, the story of Henry Warren’s ghost had seized the imaginations of Grace and Rupert and Ida, and they were unable to free themselves from its grip. Belief in ghosts was something they had never held. They had listened to ghost tales in abundance—Mary Stubbs had recounted several that were significantly more terrifying than this one; yet those stories all concerned locations and individuals and specters that were distant and unfamiliar. Once the initial sensation of awe and dread—a feeling both somewhat fearful and somewhat enjoyable—had passed, they gave them no further thought. This narrative, however, struck close to home. Almost at their own doorway—nearly within their cherished Fern Hollow—lay the old Bailey garden. Frequently they had walked past it again and again; they had searched for flowers inside it; they had used it as a shortcut whenever they desired to travel directly to the valley from the village. Yet they would do so no longer! Following the evening on which Mary Stubbs shared its ghastly account with them, they would have refused to walk through it or approach it even if threatened with death. Death! Indeed, what was death when set against the terrifying chance of being seized by the grovelling ghost of Henry Warren?
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0000 }

It was a warm evening in July when the three of them sat beneath the Tree Lovers, experiencing a slight sense of loneliness. That evening, no other person had approached the valley. Writing his entrance examinations, Kit Carrow was away in Port Marlow. Tobias and Edmund Carrow had gone out for a sail on the harbour alongside old Captain Crawford. Down the harbour road, Bess, Izzy, Tessa, and Harcourt had traveled to pay a visit to Julian and Damaris Treleaven, who had arrived with their parents to make a flying visit to the small, old House of Dreams. Although Bess had invited Grace to join them, Grace had refused. While she would not have acknowledged it to anyone, she harbored a quiet, private jealousy toward Damaris Treleaven, having heard much about her stunning beauty and city sophistication. No, she refused to travel down there and take a back seat to anyone. Accompanied by Ida, she brought her story books to Fern Hollow to read, as Rupert examined insects beside the brook's banks, and the three of them remained content until they abruptly noticed that dusk had arrived and the old Bailey garden was unsettlingly close. Rupert moved over and seated himself right beside the girls. Every one of them wished they had departed for home somewhat earlier, yet no one uttered a word.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0001 }

Enormous, plush, violet clouds piled together in the west and stretched across the valley. No breeze blew, and all became abruptly, oddly, horribly quiet. Thousands of fire-flies filled the marsh. Undoubtedly, a parliament of fairies was assembling that evening. In all respects, Fern Hollow was no safe spot right at that moment.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0002 }

Grace gazed in terror up the valley toward the old Bailey garden. At that precise instant, if the blood of any human being ever froze, Grace Ashdown’s undoubtedly did. The eyes of Rupert and Ida went where her captivated look led, and shivering dread started racing up and down their backbones as well. Positioned there beneath the large tamarack tree, upon the ruined and weed-covered embankment of the Bailey garden, rested a white object—an indistinctly white form amidst the deepening darkness. Transfixed like statues, the three Ashdowns remained seated and stared.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0003 }

“It’s—it’s the—calf,” Ida finally whispered.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0004 }

“For—the—calf, it is—too—big,” Grace whispered. Her lips and mouth had become so dry that articulating the words was nearly impossible for her.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0005 }

All at once, Rupert drew in a sharp breath,
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0006 }

“It’s coming here.”
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0007 }

The girls cast a final, anguished look. Indeed, it was crawling downward across the dyke in a manner no calf ever performed or was capable of performing. Sudden, overwhelming terror drove away all reason. At that instant, all three individuals were absolutely certain that the sight before them was the ghost of Henry Warren. Rupert jumped up and fled without direction. Screaming together, the girls pursued him. Like frantic beings, they sprinted up the slope, traversed the road, and entered the manse. They had abandoned Aunt Martha sitting in the kitchen at her sewing. She was absent. They hurried into the study. It was black and empty. Moving as if guided by a single thought, they turned about and headed toward Hollowmere—yet not by way of Fern Hollow. Descending the hill and passing along the Glen street, they sped as fast as their intense fright could carry them, with Rupert leading the way and Ida coming last. No person attempted to halt their flight, even if all who observed them marveled at the new mischief those manse children were engaged in this time. However, upon reaching the gate of Hollowmere, they collided with Clementine Ainslie, who had merely stepped inside briefly to yield back a few borrowed books.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0008 }

Her eyes took in their pale, horrified features and wide-open gaze. It dawned on her that a genuine, terrible dread, regardless of its origin, was tormenting their frail young spirits. Pulling Rupert to her side with one arm, she gathered Grace using the other. Ida lost her footing, bumping into her, and clung on with all her strength.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0009 }

“What is the matter, dear children?” she inquired. “Why are you scared?”
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0010 }

“Henry Warren’s ghost,” Rupert replied, his teeth chattering as he spoke.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0011 }

“Henry—Warren’s—ghost!” uttered bewildered Clementine, to whom the tale had never been told.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0012 }

“Yes,” Grace cried out amidst her hysteria. “It is over there—upon the Bailey embankment—we spotted it—and it began to—pursue us.”
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0013 }

Clementine ushered the three inattentive beasts toward the veranda at Hollowmere. Hugh along with Nell had left as well, having likewise departed for the House of Dreams, yet Tabitha emerged at the threshold, scrawny, sensible, and not at all like a ghost.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0014 }

“What is the cause of all this commotion?” she asked.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0015 }

Once more the children stammered through their dreadful story, as Clementine pressed them near to herself and calmed them with comforting sounds that contained no words.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0016 }

“It was probably an owl,” Tabitha remarked, completely unbothered.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0017 }

A bird of the night! From that moment on, the Ashdown kids held no respect whatsoever for the cleverness of Tabitha!
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0018 }

“It exceeded a million owls in size,” Rupert stated, weeping—oh, how embarrassed Rupert felt about that weeping in later times—“and it—it crept along precisely as Mary described—and it was slithering down across the embankment toward us. Is crawling something owls do?”
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0019 }

Clementine turned her gaze toward Tabitha.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0020 }

“Something must have scared them for them to be this frightened,” she observed.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0021 }

“I am going to check,” Tabitha remarked calmly. “Now, children, compose yourselves. It was certainly not a ghost, regardless of what you witnessed. Regarding poor Henry Warren, I am certain he would want nothing more than to repose peacefully in his tranquil grave after reaching it. He will definitely not dare to return, and you can rely on that. If you are able to persuade them to be logical, Miss Ainslie, I shall discover what is actually happening.”
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0022 }

Tabitha set off toward Fern Hollow, courageously holding a pitchfork that she discovered propped against the rear fence in the spot where the doctor had been laboring in his small hay-field. Although a pitchfork could prove ineffective against “ha’nts,” it provided a reassuring kind of protection. Upon Tabitha's arrival at Fern Hollow, there was nothing visible. No pale specters seemed to be hiding in the dark, overgrown old Bailey garden. Tabitha strode courageously across it and past it, using her pitchfork to knock on the door of the small cottage situated on the far side, the residence of Mrs. Stimson and her two daughters.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0023 }

Over at Hollowmere, Clementine was able to quiet the youngsters. They continued to weep slightly because of the fright, yet a creeping, beneficial doubt that they had behaved like utter fools was starting to take root in them. Once Tabitha at last came back, this doubt turned into a conviction.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0024 }

“I have discovered what your phantom turned out to be,” she remarked, wearing a stern grin as she sat in a rocking chair and fanned herself. “For seven days, old Mrs. Stimson had been bleaching two factory cotton sheets inside the Bailey garden. Because the turf was tidy and brief in that spot, she laid them across the embankment beneath the tamarack tree. She ventured outside to retrieve them tonight. Carrying her knitting in her hands, she draped the sheets across her shoulders to transport them. Subsequently, she must have lost one of her needles, which she was unable to locate and still has not found. Nevertheless, she got down on her knees and crawled around searching for it, and that was her exact occupation when she heard terrible screams down in the valley and observed the three children racing up the slope right by her. Believing something had bitten them, her frail old heart suffered such a shock that she was incapable of moving or uttering a word, merely remaining stooped there until they went out of sight. Afterwards, she stumbled back to her house where they have been administering remedies to her continually, and her heart remains in a dreadful state, with her declaring that this scare will affect her for the rest of the summer.”
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0025 }

The Ashdowns remained seated, red with a humiliation that not even the compassionate understanding of Clementine was able to dispel. They crept away toward their house, encountered Tobias by the gate of the manse, and offered a penitent confession. For the following morning, a meeting of the Good-Conduct Club was set up.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0026 }

From her bed, Grace softly asked, “Didn’t Miss Ainslie treat us so kindly this evening?”
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0027 }

“Yes,” Ida acknowledged. “The transformation that people undergo upon becoming stepmothers is truly unfortunate.”
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0028 }

“I do not think it does,” Grace replied with loyalty.
{: #nw-v05-c30-p0029 }
